drapeaux.note: Serment de Louis (842), en langue romane (ancêtre du français), laissé tel quel : Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo et nostro commun salvament.
Gloses du serment de Louis et mots de Nithard (« en langue romane », « parce qu'il était l'aîné »), rendus depuis le français ; originaux en roman et en latin, auteur Nithard.

accroche: On February 14, 842, two kings swear an alliance, each in the language of the other's army. The text has reached us only through a late copy.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 14, 842, in Strasbourg, two grandsons of Charlemagne swear loyalty to each other before their assembled armies. Louis the German and Charles the Bald had just defeated their elder brother Lothair at Fontenoy, in June 841, and want to stand together against him. We know the scene from a single witness: Nithard, an adviser to Charles, who recounts the event in his *Histories*, in Latin.

## Two Oaths, Two Languages

Nithard reports that Charles first gives a speech “in the Romance language.” Louis, “because he was the elder,” swears first: he does so in the Romance language (*romana lingua*), so that Charles's army will understand him. Charles then repeats the same words in the Germanic language (*teudisca lingua*), that of Louis's army. The two armies then swear in turn, each in its own language. The chronicler gives the text of each oath as it was spoken.

Louis's oath begins like this: *Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo et nostro commun salvament*, “for the love of God and for the salvation of the Christian people and our common salvation.” The choice of languages is political: an oath the army does not understand binds no one.

## What the Text Is, and What It Is Not

This passage is often presented as the birth certificate of French. It is also often presented as the first text in a Romance language, but several clarifications are needed. Nithard himself writes *romana lingua*, the “Romance language,” and does not speak of French. The text does not survive in an original from the 9th century: we know it from a manuscript of Nithard's work copied at the end of the 10th century, now held in the Bibliothèque nationale de France (National Library of France), Latin 9768. Finally, what we have before us is a language written down by a cleric. According to Wikipedia's page on the subject, philologists have tried to tie it to a specific dialect (Picard, Lyonnais, Lower Lorraine, or Poitevin, depending on the author), without reaching agreement. Several scholars see it instead as a kind of koine of northern France, a common written language of an artificial character, close to a chancery language, rather than the speech of one region faithfully recorded.

## The Shift

A treaty of this importance is no longer drafted in Latin but in the languages of the peoples, according to the Deutsches Historisches Museum. The choice of two languages also shows that in 842 the two armies no longer spoke the same language. We do not know how many soldiers actually understood the oath they were made to pronounce.

repere.texte: The Oaths of Strasbourg of February 14, 842 are known to us from a manuscript, copied at the end of the 10th century, of Nithard's *Histoire des fils de Louis le Pieux* (*History of the Sons of Louis the Pious*), now held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France under shelfmark Latin 9768.
repere.source: Lexilogos, “Strasbourg Oaths” (Nithard's text and reference for the BnF Latin 9768 manuscript)

carte.punch: The first text in a Romance language is, they say, a military oath, made to be understood.
carte.idee: On February 14, 842, Louis swears in the Romance language and Charles in the Germanic language, each in the language of the other's army. The text is known to us from a copy, made at the end of the 10th century, of Nithard's Histories.
carte.source_courte: Nithard, Histories, Book III; BnF Latin 9768

quiz.question: Why does Louis swear in the Romance language and Charles in the Germanic language?
choix: Because each king spoke the language of the other's army and wanted to show courtesy by using it
Because each addresses the other's army in the language it understands, so that the oath binds it
Because Latin was banned from military acts by a decree of Charlemagne
Because each king had to swear in the language of his own army, according to Frankish custom
quiz.explication: According to Nithard, each speaks in the language of the army he is addressing, which is that of the other king. The point is that the oath be understood: it is not a matter of courtesy, it is not imposed by a decree, and the king does not swear in the language of his own army.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How have the Oaths of Strasbourg come down to us?
choix: Through an original parchment signed in 842
Through a copy, made at the end of the 10th century, of Nithard's work
Through a treaty kept in the archives of Strasbourg
Through the song of a 9th-century minstrel
quiz_supplementaire.explication: No original act is known: the text appears in manuscript BnF Latin 9768, a copy made at the end of the 10th century of Nithard's Histories.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What word does Nithard use for the language of Louis's oath?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Nithard writes romana lingua. The name “French” does not appear in his text; it was applied to this language later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What relation are Louis the German and Charles the Bald to Charlemagne?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: They are two grandsons of Charlemagne, sons of Louis the Pious, allied against their elder brother Lothair.
